title: Washington's Growing Portfolio: Tracking U.S. Government Investments
date_evidence: Published April 22, 2026 10:45 a.m. ... Jonathan E. Hillman, Senior Fellow for Geoeconomics
key_claim: CFR's U.S. Government Deal Tracker records that since January 2025 the federal government has invested $20.9 billion across 16 deals involving direct equity ownership, including a 10 percent stake in Intel and a golden share in U.S. Steel; Congress has expanded the Development Finance Corporation's investment ceiling from $60 billion to $205 billion and broadened its authority to take equity, and the government has mobilised an additional $4.75 billion in private co-investment alongside partners including the Emirati sovereign wealth fund ADQ.
frame_summary: Argues the U.S. government is making equity ownership a standing tool of industrial policy and economic security, acquiring stakes, warrants and golden shares across strategic sectors.
notes: Primary quantification anchor for the scale of the U.S. state-equity turn.

title: Follow the Money: Finance and the Future of Allied Economic Statecraft
date_evidence: Georgie Skipper March 25, 2026 ... War by Other Ledgers
key_claim: War on the Rocks argues that the ability to mobilise and direct large pools of public and private capital is becoming the defining instrument of economic statecraft, pointing to a new toolkit of state investment vehicles (the U.S. DoD Office of Strategic Capital deploying roughly $1.2 billion, the NATO Innovation Fund launched with about $1.2 billion from 24 allies, and Gulf funds Mubadala, ADIA, Saudi Arabia's PIF and the Qatar Investment Authority) through which states crowd private capital into strategic sectors.
frame_summary: Argues finance and state-directed capital have become the central instrument of contemporary economic statecraft, and that allies must organise their capital stack to compete.
notes: Institutional anchor for the 'capital as statecraft' framing and the allied/Gulf dimension.

title: Investment and Statecraft: The International Politics of Sovereign Wealth Funds
key_claim: Political economist Kathryn Lavelle argues that sovereign wealth funds, of which more than 100 now exist, invest on behalf of governments in a way that embeds a contest between the state's interests and financial returns, that it is often unclear who makes their decisions and for what purposes, and that a U.S. sovereign wealth fund, for which the Trump administration announced a plan, would carry tremendous weight while cutting against the U.S. tradition of separating political and investment functions.
frame_summary: Argues sovereign wealth funds fuse state purpose with market investment in opaque ways, and that a U.S. fund would mark a significant change in how Washington practises economic statecraft.
notes: Provides the analytical frame on the sovereign-versus-wealth tension and the global SWF context.

title: US Explores State Capitalism
key_claim: CEPA argues that to compete with China, Washington is taking minority equity stakes in firms critical to semiconductors, rare earths and lithium as a stabilising anchor that deters foreign takeovers and crowds in private investment, citing the U.S. 9.9 percent stake in Intel and the Defense Department becoming MP Materials' largest shareholder, alongside European precedents such as Germany's 17 percent stake in Uniper, while warning that state ownership invites political interference.
frame_summary: Argues U.S. minority equity stakes are a deliberate, non-controlling tool to safeguard strategically vital firms, echoing European precedents but carrying real risks of politicised capital allocation.
notes: Canonical framing source for the U.S. state-capitalism turn and its European parallels.

title: The Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS): Known Investor Program RFI
date_evidence: Evergreen CFIUS programme page; states that on 6 February 2026 Treasury issued a Request for Information on the Known Investor Program and streamlining the foreign investment review process, with the public comment period closing 18 March 2026.
key_claim: The U.S. Treasury's CFIUS, operating under section 721 of the Defense Production Act, issued a Request for Information on 6 February 2026 on a Known Investor Program to streamline the foreign investment review process for trusted investors while preserving rigorous national-security screening, with the comment period closing 18 March 2026.
frame_summary: Shows the U.S. government formalising a split between trusted and adversary capital in inbound investment review, the screening counterpart to its outbound equity stakes.
notes: Tier 1 primary government source for the inbound-screening / trusted-capital dimension of the signal.

title: Trump's State Capitalism, by the Numbers
date_evidence: WebSearch result: foreignpolicy.com/2026/01/14/trump-state-capitalism-equity-stakes-list-companies — 'Trump's State Capitalism: List of Companies, Sectors'
key_claim: Foreign Policy catalogues the nearly dozen firms in which the Trump administration has taken a government stake or a share of profits, including a roughly 10 percent stake worth nearly $11 billion in Intel, a 15 percent Defense Department stake in MP Materials with a magnet offtake and price floor, a 40 percent stake in a Korea Zinc refinery, a golden share in U.S. Steel, and a 25 percent cut of Nvidia's China chip sales.
frame_summary: Argues that taking direct stakes in strategic firms is the clearest sign of the Trump administration's turn to state capitalism, a trend set to accelerate through 2026.
notes: Deal-by-deal quantification of the U.S. equity portfolio; date taken from the dated article URL via WebSearch.

title: Trump Says The US Government May Take Equity Stakes In OpenAI And xAI
key_claim: Tech Times reports that on 5 June 2026 President Trump said the federal government may take direct equity stakes in OpenAI, Anthropic and xAI via an OpenAI-proposed 'Public Wealth Fund' seeded by donated shares, that Senator Bernie Sanders has called for 50 percent government stakes plus a 50 percent tax on those firms, and that Anthropic has declined to participate, illustrating a cross-ideological convergence toward government ownership of frontier AI.
frame_summary: Argues government ownership of frontier AI has moved from fringe proposal to live policy with support from both Trump and Sanders, raising the regulator-owns-the-regulated conflict.
notes: Freshest evidence of the frontier extending to AI, plus the left-right convergence and a built-in for/against.

title: Trump's Presidential Portfolio Goes Quantum
key_claim: The Cato Institute argues that the administration's roughly $2 billion in CHIPS-Act quantum-computing deals for nine companies, including about $1 billion for IBM in exchange for equity, distort competition, politicise investment and build a patronage market, noting that U.S.-headquartered quantum firms already raised more than $2.7 billion in venture capital in 2025 and that IBM is not a fragile startup.
frame_summary: Argues the state-equity spree is improvised, market-distorting cronyism that picks winners and entangles government with firms it regulates, and is unnecessary given deep private capital.
notes: Counter-argument source: the strongest free-market critique of the state-as-shareholder turn.
